questions.question: James Lind took twelve sailors sick with scurvy aboard the Salisbury in 1747, picking cases 'as similar as I could have them'. All twelve shared one sick berth and one diet, and each pair got its own remedy, from cider and vinegar to seawater and two oranges and a lemon a day. In six days one of the fruit pair was fit for duty; no other pair mended so fast. What could the other five pairs rule out?
questions.answer: That rest and the ship's food alone had healed the two
choices: That rest and the ship's food alone had healed the two
That luck alone had made those two mend faster
That those two had been the mildest cases to begin with
That the oranges alone would have healed the two as fast
questions.context: All twelve had the same rest and the same food, so if those had done the healing, the other ten would have mended as fast, and they did not. With only two men a pair, the trial could not rule out luck or a difference in the men themselves, and since the fruit pair ate oranges and a lemon together, it could not say which fruit did the work. Lind wrote that oranges and lemons were 'the most effectual remedies for this distemper at sea'.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn what a comparison group rules out and what it leaves open, and Lind's six pairs are the classic early case.

questions.question: James Lind decided for himself which of his twelve scurvy patients got each remedy aboard the Salisbury in 1747. He gave the seawater to 'the worst patients', the only two whose tendons behind the knee had gone stiff. A doctor can instead match his groups with care, so that each holds as many of the very sick as the other. Fair trials today leave the choice to chance. What does chance do that careful matching cannot?
questions.answer: It evens out, on average, differences no one checked
choices: It evens out, on average, differences no one checked
It makes the two groups alike in every way
It makes the patients a fair sample of all the sick
It keeps each patient from knowing his own treatment
questions.context: Matching evens out only the differences a doctor thinks to check, such as how sick each patient is, while chance also evens out, on average, the ones no one thought of; it never makes two groups alike in every way, and small groups can still differ by luck. In the 1948 trial of streptomycin that Austin Bradford Hill helped design, random numbers sealed in envelopes put each patient in a group, so no doctor could steer the sickest into one. Chance only sorts the patients a trial already has, so it does not make them a fair sample of all the sick, and it hides no one's treatment: that is the work of blinding.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design teaches confounding variables and sample selection, and random assignment, set against matching by hand, is the standard answer to the differences no one measured.

questions.question: James Lind's twelve sailors aboard the Salisbury pointed to oranges and lemons, and he wrote the trial up in A Treatise of the Scurvy in 1753. Later, as physician at the naval hospital at Haslar, he wrote that lemon juice had relieved 'many hundred patients'. Which view did Lind hold?
questions.answer: Scurvy has several causes, damp air among them
choices: Scurvy has several causes, damp air among them
Scurvy comes from the lack of one thing in the diet
Lemon juice boiled down to a syrup loses its power
Scurvy is cured by fresh fruit and nothing else
questions.context: Lind shared the view of his day that scurvy had several causes, such as salt meat eaten in damp air that held back sweating, and saw it as a fault of digestion rather than a lack in the diet, so he read his own result through that theory and kept recommending other remedies too. He even boiled lemon juice into a 'rob' to carry to sea, not knowing that the boiling destroyed the vitamin C that cures scurvy. The trial filled only a few paragraphs of his long book, and the Royal Navy issued lemon juice to every warship only in 1795, urged on by Gilbert Blane.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that evidence is read through the ideas a scientist already holds, and Lind's own book is the honest after-story of his trial.

questions.question: Surgeons once treated angina, chest pain when the heart gets too little blood, by tying off two arteries in the chest wall, and early reports said most patients improved. Leonard Cobb's team in Seattle tested the operation in 1959 on 17 patients: 8 had the arteries tied, and 9 had only the same cuts in the skin. The patients were not told which they had. About as many improved in each group. What did the trial show?
questions.answer: The tying of the arteries added nothing to the relief
choices: The tying of the arteries added nothing to the relief
Both the tying and the skin cuts had mended the heart
The patients' chest pain had been imagined all along
Any small operation on the chest can cure angina
questions.context: The sham patients improved just as often, so the relief came from something other than the tying: the hope an operation brings, the care around it, or pain that eases by itself. Nothing showed that either operation mended a heart, and angina is real pain from a heart short of blood. A second trial against a sham operation, by Dimond's team in 1960, found the tying no better, and surgeons soon gave the operation up.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge a claim by its control group, and the sham operation is the clearest case of a placebo arm showing what a treatment really adds.

questions.question: Henry Beecher, a Harvard anaesthetist, gathered fifteen trials in his 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' and reported that about a third of their patients were relieved by a dummy pill alone. Gunver Kienle and Helmut Kiene went back to the same trials in 1997 and found no evidence of a placebo effect in any of them. Set beside the dummy-pill patients, which group would have shown what the dummy itself did?
questions.answer: Patients given no pill at all, followed the same way
choices: Patients given no pill at all, followed the same way
Patients given the real drug, followed the same way
Patients told openly that their pill was a dummy
Healthy people given the dummy pill, followed the same way
questions.context: Sick people often get better on their own, symptoms come and go, and patients enrolled at their worst tend to improve, so a dummy-pill group holds all of that as well as any effect of the pill. Only a group given nothing, followed in the same way, shows what the dummy itself adds, and Beecher's trials had none. Setting a dummy pill beside a real drug measures the drug, not the dummy.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks which comparison a claim needs, and the placebo is the textbook case where the missing no-treatment group changed the answer.

questions.question: Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche gathered 114 trials in 2001, covering about 40 different illnesses, in which some patients got a placebo and others got no treatment at all. What did they find that the placebos had done?
questions.answer: Small effects on what patients felt, such as pain
choices: Small effects on what patients felt, such as pain
Small effects on what tests measured, such as blood pressure
Large effects on what patients felt, such as pain
Large effects on what tests measured, such as blood pressure
questions.context: The review found that, against no treatment, placebos did nothing measurable to the illnesses themselves, while patients given them reported a little less pain. By that measure a dummy pill can ease how people feel, a little, and much of the improvement seen in placebo groups comes from getting better anyway; how large placebo effects are is still argued.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders meet the placebo effect in biology and health, and this review is the honest measure of how far it reaches.

questions.question: Steven Cummings's team scanned the hips of women taking a medicine for osteoporosis, thinning of the bones, once a year. In most women the medicine makes the hip bone a little denser each year, but each scan carries some chance error. The team picked out the women whose scans showed a loss of more than 4 percent in the first year. Kept on the same medicine, what did most of them show in the second year?
choices: A gain in hip bone
Another loss about as large
A smaller loss than the first
No change in hip bone
questions.context: Women picked out for a big first-year loss were partly picked out by scans that had read low by chance, so their next change swung back toward the usual gain: 83 percent gained bone in the second year, while women who had gained 8 percent or more in the first year lost a little in the second. This regression to the mean is why one year's scan can mislead a doctor into changing a medicine that works, and why a dramatic recovery proves little without a comparison group.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks students to evaluate explanations against the data, and regression to the mean is the standard reason a dramatic recovery or a single bad reading is not by itself evidence.

questions.question: John Noseworthy's team reported in 1994 on a Canadian trial of treatments for multiple sclerosis, a disease of the brain and spinal cord. Some patients had plasma exchange, which swaps out the liquid part of the blood, and some a sham, a fake exchange. At every check-up two neurologists examined each patient: one knew the patient's treatment, and one did not. Only the neurologists who knew scored the plasma-exchange patients as doing better than the sham patients. What does this show?
questions.answer: Knowing the treatment had tilted the doctors' scores
choices: Knowing the treatment had tilted the doctors' scores
The blinded doctors had missed a benefit the others saw
The patients' belief in the treatment had made them better
The sham treatment had made its patients worse
questions.context: Both neurologists examined the same patients at the same visits, so the gap could come only from the examiners, and only one of them had a reason to be swayed. Judged blind, neither treatment beat the sham, and the authors wrote that blinding the doctors had saved them from a false conclusion. A doctor who knows can tilt a result without meaning to, in how he judges a doubtful case or how he cares for a patient.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science values objectivity and asks why a double-blind trial hides the treatment from the doctor as well as the patient; this trial measured the difference directly.

questions.question: Paralytic polio struck about 57 of every 100,000 children given a dummy shot in the 1954 field trial of Jonas Salk's vaccine, and 16 in 100,000 of those given the vaccine. Suppose a single school had run the same test on its own 1,000 children, half given the vaccine and half the dummy, and no child in either half got paralytic polio. What would the school's result show?
questions.answer: Nothing either way, as so few cases were to be expected
choices: Nothing either way, as so few cases were to be expected
That the vaccine failed, since the dummy half did as well
That polio had not reached the school that season
That the school's children were already immune to polio
questions.context: At those rates the school could expect less than a third of a case among its 500 dummy-shot children, and fewer among the vaccinated, so a season with no cases at all was the likeliest outcome however well the vaccine worked, and it says nothing about whether polio came near or the children were immune. Paralytic polio was rare even in a bad year, so it is the number of cases, not of children, that decides what such a trial can show, which is why Thomas Francis's trial enrolled about 1.8 million children.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design asks how much data a test needs and what a result without a gap can show, and a rare disease is the clearest case where the number of cases, not of people, decides it.

questions.question: In the areas of the 1954 polio trial that used a dummy shot, children whose parents asked to join got either the vaccine or the dummy, and children whose parents refused got nothing. Paralytic polio struck the dummy-shot children at 57 in every 100,000, but the refused children at only 36. In the areas with no dummy shots, second-graders whose parents refused also fell ill less often than the first and third grades, watched as controls. What did these gaps show?
questions.answer: Families who sign up differ from those who do not
choices: Families who sign up differ from those who do not
The dummy shot itself had raised the risk of polio
Chance alone had made the rates differ
The dummy shot had been a weak dose of the vaccine
questions.context: Families who volunteered were on the whole better off, and polio seemed to strike hardest where homes were cleanest, so their children ran a higher risk from the start, shot or no shot, as the areas without dummy shots showed; a dummy that held weak vaccine would have lowered the dummy group's rate, and with over 200 cases between the two groups, the gap was too wide for chance. So the dummy-shot areas, which compared volunteers with volunteers, were the stronger test. There the vaccinated fell ill at 16 in 100,000 against the dummy group's 57, a cut of about 72 percent; counting only the cases a laboratory confirmed, Thomas Francis put the vaccine at 80 to 90 percent effective against paralytic polio.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that sample selection limits what a comparison can show, and the polio trial's two designs set the volunteer problem and its cure side by side.

The wrong choices are the real confusions: groups alike in every way, random sampling, blinding.

The context ends on the nature-of-science point (judge low).

Now the student must work the expected cases (under a third of a case in 500 at 57 per 100,000) to read a small school's no-case result, against the misreadings that it shows the vaccine failed, that polio stayed away, or that the children were immune: the T5 point that cases, not children, decide, and that no gap in a test too small to see one shows nothing.
